newsitem.title: UK: Camilla steps out of shadows as royal lover.
newsitem.headline: Camilla steps out of shadows as royal lover.

text.p: Camilla Parker Bowles, the royal mistress behind the British throne, stepped out of the shadows at a glittering 50th birthday party hosted by her lover Prince Charles.

In an unprecedented declaration of commitment to the woman he has secretly loved for 25 years, Charles threw a champagne party on Friday for about 100 guests at his Highgrove country home -- and all but invited the world to join in.

A radiant Parker Bowles, sporting a chunky diamond and gold necklace and black sleeveless dress, found herself on the front pages of almost every British newspaper on Saturday after the most publicly-scrutinised private party of the year.

"Camilla's a thriller" trumpeted the Daily Mirror, noting how police and the future British king paved the way for waiting photographers and television crews to take pictures of Camilla as she arrived for an evening of dancing and feasting on the lawns of Charles's rural retreat.
Gone was the frowning frump blamed by the vast majority of Britons for wrecking the 1981 marriage of Prince Charles and the glamorous Princess Diana.

With a new hairdo and a broad smile, the usually publicity-shy Parker Bowles beamed with a confidence unseen during the dark years when her affair with the heir to the throne seemed to threaten the very institution of monarchy.
"She looked like a debutante on her first big night out, finally ready to take centre stage," said the Daily Mirror.
Conscious of hostile public opinion just a year after the prince and princess divorced, Charles and Camilla have never been photographed together, let alone appeared in public together.

Friday night was no exception but the discreet campaign to improve Parker Bowles's image and convince the British public that she is a permanent fixture in Charles's life appears to be showing results.

One opinion poll last week showed that 68 percent of Britons were now in favour of Charles and Camilla marrying -- although Charles, compromised by his dual role on assuming the crown as supreme governor of the Church of England, has said he has no plans to do so.

Significantly no members of the royal family attended the party, whose guests included novelist Jilly Cooper and broadcaster Melyvn Bragg as well as the ex-husband of Parker Bowles, their two grown-up children and her father.
Princess Diana, who once dubbed Parker Bowles "the Rottweiler", kept her distance on holiday in the south of France.

The party enjoyed a five-course dinner in a marquee and were serenaded by classical musicians. Rumours that New Zealand soprano Kiri Te Kanawa, who sang at the ill-fated royal wedding, was to lead a chorus of "Happy Birthday", proved unfounded.
Labour MP Tony Wright on Friday signalled growing public acceptance of the relationship, saying "the sky would not fall in" if the prince re-married.
"Life will continue," Wright told BBC radio. "Most people in this country would rather have a happy monarch than an unhappy monarch."
